Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
Kofi once carried himself with an easy authority, a quality that served him well in his work as a parole officer. Now, at 34, that confidence has been replaced by a quiet, gnawing tension that seems to hum just beneath his skin. The change began eight months ago, after the night his then-partner, Mark, attacked him in their shared apartment. The assault was a blur of betrayal and violence, ending with a trip to the emergency room. It is the sensory details of that night, and its immediate aftermath, that have become the architecture of his fear. The specific way Mark had looked at him just before, a gaze that stripped him of his personhood, now makes any hint of sexual objectification feel like a physical threat. The antiseptic smell of the hospital where his lip was stitched has clung to his olfactory memory, turning the sterile scent of his own government office building into a minefield.

These triggers are not simply reminders; they are portals. A routine check-in at work, where he must sit alone in a small room with a male parolee, can become an exercise in terror. The combination of the man's presence and the faint, clean smell of the building is enough to send him spiraling. Each time it happens, the trigger delivers a fresh judgment, telling him with a logic he cannot argue with that his life has been fundamentally destroyed. This sensory input immediately activates a profound sense of threat; Kofi's body clenches, his fists tightening under the table as he begins scanning the other man's face and posture for any sign of aggression. Simultaneously, the trigger yanks the memory into the present. He isn't just remembering; he can hear the low, cruel words Mark spoke during the assault, and the coppery taste of blood fills his mouth as if the injury were fresh. The memory feels so immediate, so viscerally present, that his body reacts as if the danger is happening all over again, his heart hammering against his ribs. Feeling this afraid all the time, he has eventually come to accept the conclusion his body keeps offering: that he is not the kind of person who gets to feel safe anymore. This state of high alert, in turn, makes the memories more accessible and vivid, creating a feedback loop where the more threatened he feels, the more intensely he relives the trauma.

This constant bombardment has reshaped his view of himself and the world. He has come to believe that his life has been fundamentally destroyed by the trauma, a conviction of profound injustice that poisons his every interaction. This conviction that the world is now an unsafe place means he moves through his days as if they are mined-every ambiguity, from a stranger's prolonged gaze to footsteps behind him on the street, has become a potential signal of attack. The feeling that his life is no longer worth living surfaces often, a flat, hopeless conclusion. These dark appraisals are the engine of his daily behaviour. Believing his life is ruined, any flicker of joy or affection from his new partner feels like a dangerous lie, an opening for more pain, so he instinctively pushes it away. This core belief that what happened was deeply unfair makes him see potential perpetrators everywhere, turning every man he is alone with into a source of potent danger.

From this place of fear and negative conviction, a host of protective strategies have emerged, each one tightening the trap. He assiduously avoids eye contact with others, especially the men on his caseload, and sidesteps any situation that might lead to conflict, often conceding points at work just to end a conversation. These safety behaviors have effectively drawn a map of the event around him; the very act of averting his gaze now serves as its own reminder, turning every unreadable male face into a new source of potential danger. But these attempts to manage the threat only feed it. Avoiding eye contact leaves him guessing at others' intentions, a void his mind fills with the worst-case scenario, keeping his body on constant alert. His attempts to suppress positive emotions leave a vacuum that the intrusive memories rush to fill, often catching him off guard with their auditory and gustatory vividness. The memories themselves reinforce his belief that he is permanently damaged, which then fuels his drive to avoid any potential trigger or emotional risk. His world has shrunk into a series of carefully managed corridors, designed to prevent the past from erupting into the present.

The consequences have been stark. His supervisor has noted his increasing detachment and reluctance to handle difficult cases. His new partner, Amina, feels him slipping away, walled off behind a barrier of anxious vigilance she cannot breach. It was after she found him sitting motionless in his car for an hour, unable to enter their apartment after a difficult day at work, that he finally agreed to seek help. Kofi came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate, terrifying question: what if he is right, and his life really has been destroyed for good?

violations.explanation: The vignette does not state that encountering triggers directly activates the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world.
The vignette does not state that the patient's negative beliefs cause him to become more sensitive to or develop new triggers.
The vignette does not state that the patient's feeling of threat causes or reinforces his negative beliefs.
The vignette does not state that the patient's avoidance behaviours make him more sensitive to or create new triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that encountering triggers directly activates the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not state that the patient's negative beliefs cause him to become more sensitive to or develop new triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not state that the patient's feeling of threat causes or reinforces his negative beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not state that the patient's avoidance behaviours make him more sensitive to or create new triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
